1.goal: To open on the exact moment: she has stopped talking, and somebody has raised a hand.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese works here — the question is what matters.
run: Ask which question has caught her by surprise after a presentation.
If she did lesson 3, remind her: it was she who said nobody had answered “which regulator”. That is the first question today.
1.expected: One question she remembers being asked, and why it caught her.
1.support: If nothing comes, ask about a question she saw someone else fail to answer.
1.challenge: Ask what she wishes she had said, and what stopped her from saying it.
1.monitoring: Whether the example is a question she could not answer or one she answered badly. They are different problems.
1.evidence: The question she names — it is the scene the lesson gives back.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one concrete example.

2.goal: To establish who is in the room and what each of them can do with the answer.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the situation on screen together.
run: Give her time to read.
Confirm out loud: there are three questions, and she answers one at a time.
2.expected: That Diane has the vote, and that the three are not asking for the same thing.
2.support: If the roles blur, ask what each of the three does on Monday with the answer she gives.
2.challenge: Ask which of the three she would rather answer last, and why.
2.monitoring: Do not anticipate that one of them is hostile. Discovering that by listening is stage 4.
2.evidence: Whether she identifies who decides before hearing the questions.
2.transition: Move on when she says which of the three decides.

3.goal: To risk a hypothesis about what is coming, before hearing it.
3.interaction: T–S, one prediction, then one listening.
run: Read the line on screen out loud and ask the question.
Accept ANY guess; do not confirm and do not correct.
Then play the first question ONCE.
exact: The two options, if she will not commit: “Agree with you, or find the hole?”
3.expected: Either answer is fine. What you want is that she commits before hearing.
3.support: If she will not commit, offer the two options and let her pick one.
3.challenge: Ask what the first six words would have to be for it to be the other one.
3.monitoring: The prediction exists to activate what she already knows. If you confirm the guess, she stops risking on the next ones.
3.evidence: Whether she risks a hypothesis at all. It is the habit the block works on.
3.transition: Move on when she has risked a guess and heard it once.

4.goal: To hear the three once and notice that they are not asking for the same thing.
4.interaction: S listens to all three without pause, then marks alone.
run: Play the three in a row, with no pause and NO transcript.
Then the exercise.
exact: Did any of them ask you to repeat the recommendation? (None.)
4.expected: The two that ask for something she has not said, marked correctly.
4.support: If she asks for the transcript, hold it until stage 5. The difficulty here is part of the task.
4.challenge: Ask which of the three she could answer with a number, before hearing them again.
4.monitoring: Whether she separates the three by what they ask for, or by tone.
4.evidence: What one listening gives her without support. It is the first listening measure of the cycle.
4.transition: Move on when she marks the two right ones, with or without a second listening.

5.goal: To attribute each statement to whoever said it — and to find the one nobody said.
5.interaction: S works alone, then T–S on the limit case.
run: Play again, one question at a time if needed.
Let her work alone and only then open the explanation.
exact: Who gave you a number you did not have? (Diane, the four months.)
Who asked you to confirm the recommendation? (Nobody.)
5.expected: One of the six was said by none of them, and finding it is the point.
5.support: If an attribution will not come, play only the turn it depends on and ask who is speaking before asking what they want.
5.challenge: Ask what she would have to say differently if Diane had asked Nadia's question.
5.monitoring: The “none of them” item is what decides the lesson: the room has already heard the request, and repeating the recommendation wastes the first sentence.
5.evidence: Whether she catches the limit case on her own. It predicts the opening of her answers at stage 8.
5.transition: Move on when she gets the limit case right.

6.goal: To separate the three things an answer does before it answers: buying time, checking, disagreeing.
6.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S on the two questions.
run: She classifies, then open the explanation.
Ask: which of these say NOTHING about the content? (The two that buy time.) And what are they for, then?
exact: Does “That is a fair question” answer anything? (No.) So what is it for? (Four seconds to decide the shape of the answer.)
6.expected: Two of the six buy time, two check, two disagree — and only the last four carry content.
6.support: If a line resists, ask whether the person asking learns anything from it.
6.challenge: Ask for one more time-buying line of her own, in her register.
6.monitoring: She may think buying time sounds unsure. It is the opposite: whoever does it never looks like they are searching.
6.evidence: Whether she names the time-buying column as the one that carries no content.
6.transition: Move on when she names the time-buying column as the one that carries no content.

7.goal: To produce the check out loud, with support on screen.
7.interaction: T asks short vague questions; S gives back only the check. Six, at speed.
run: Ask deliberately short and vague questions; she gives back only the check, without answering.
Seven minutes, and the next stage is the longest. If she starts actually answering, cut in.
Pronunciation: “If I understand you CORrectly” — the peak is on COR, and the rest runs fast. “Fair” is one long syllable, not two.
exact: If she starts answering: “Only the check — do not answer yet.”
7.expected: Six checks, none of them containing an answer.
7.support: If the check will not come, give the first three words and let her finish.
7.challenge: Ask a question that is vague in two different ways and ask for a check that names both.
7.monitoring: Whether the check stays a check, or slides into the answer.
7.evidence: On how many of the six she produces the check without the screen.
7.transition: Move on when she produces the check without looking at the screen on the last two.

8.goal: The product of the lesson — answering the three, live, one at a time.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are Diane, then Ray, then Nadia.
run: Ask each question OUT LOUD, not from the screen. Wait for the whole answer before moving to the next.
The turn is hers. Do not finish her sentence and do not suggest the word — the silence is work.
On the hostile one, keep the pressure: if she retreats, repeat the objection once. Retreating from the objection is the point this lesson exists to work on.
Do not correct during. Note it and hand it back at stage 9.
exact: Repeating the hostile objection, without softening it: “I still do not see how that holds. Say it again.”
Handing over the turn: “Nadia, your question.”
8.expected: Three answers, each opening with a check or with four seconds — never with the recommendation repeated.
8.support: If she goes blank on the hostile one, repeat only the objection and wait. Do not offer language.
8.challenge: Add a fourth question from Diane at the end, in one sentence, and take the answer inside a minute.
8.monitoring: How each answer opens, and what happens to the check under the hostile question.
8.evidence: One answer as she gave it, word for word — it is the third field of the next screen.
8.transition: Move on when the three have been answered, or at twelve minutes.

9.goal: To hand back two points and to ask for the hostile one again, with less time.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the board together, then one replay.
run: Two things, no more.
Then: Nadia again, and this time twenty seconds.
Do not add new content. The replay is the same task under one changed constraint.
exact: Nadia again — and this time you have twenty seconds.
9.expected: The same answer with the two parts collapsed into one, and the check still there.
9.support: If twenty seconds will not fit, ask which half of the answer Nadia already has.
9.challenge: Ask for it once more in ten seconds and see what survives twice.
9.monitoring: Whether, with less time, she cuts the CHECK. If she does, the check is not automatic yet.
9.evidence: What she cut. It goes in the post-lesson record and is decided in lesson 6, which closes the block.
9.transition: Move on when the twenty-second version has been given.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the close.
run: She ticks what she recognizes. Do not argue with the marks.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has one optional recording about the hardest question she has ever been asked, and two TED talks.
Announce lesson 5: it is the grammar one, and it is not revision. It is the syntax under the markers — why “what this means is” works and “this means” does not work the same way.
exact: The Joy Buolamwini talk is from her field, and it is worth noticing how many times she repeats the question before answering it.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, ask which line she would have wanted in the last Q&A she faced.
10.challenge: Ask when the next presentation with questions is, and which of the three moves she takes into it.
10.monitoring: A low mark on the hostile question after an answer that held is worth recording: it is the gap between doing and knowing that she did.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record BEFORE you close. This is the first listening and interaction measure of the cycle.
